title: The Business of Wine
description: How wine is made into a product, priced, sold and collected, and what climate change means for all of it.
L: Describe the route from producer to consumer

A bottle passes through several hands. The producer sells to an importer or distributor, who sells to retailers and restaurants, who sell to you. Each step adds a margin. Large producers may also sell directly through cellar doors, clubs and online, keeping more of the price.

In the United States, a law from 1933, after Prohibition, created the three-tier system: producers must sell to wholesalers, who sell to retailers or restaurants. Each state sets its own rules, and some sell alcohol only through state-run shops. In many other markets, importers and distributors play similar roles, but with fewer legal restrictions.
What does the US three-tier system require?
Producers sell to wholesalers, who sell to retailers
Only state shops may sell wine
The system separates producers, wholesalers and retailers, though some states allow exceptions.

Off-trade means shops and supermarkets, where most wine is sold. On-trade means restaurants and bars, with higher margins. Direct to consumer includes cellar doors, wine clubs and online sales. Supermarkets dominate volume in the UK and much of Europe; on-trade shapes a wine's image.
Match each channel to its description.
Each channel has different margins and roles.
Wine moves from producer through importers and retailers
The US uses a legal three-tier system
Off-trade, on-trade and direct sales are the main channels
Explain how a bottle's price is built
Explain why cheap wine has little wine value

A bottle's price includes grapes, winemaking, packaging, transport, duty, tax, and the margins of each seller. In the UK, duty on a 750 ml bottle at 11 to 14.5% was about 2.67 pounds in 2023, plus 20% VAT. On a 6 pound bottle, the wine itself may be worth less than 1 pound. Fixed costs weigh most on cheap wine.
Fixed costs weigh on cheap wine

Higher prices reflect lower yields, hand labour, steep slopes, oak barrels, long ageing and scarcity. Above a certain level, prices follow reputation and demand rather than cost. A Grand Cru Burgundy costs hundreds of pounds because the vineyard is tiny and global demand is high, not because it costs that much to make.
Cost up to a point, then scarcity
On a cheap bottle, most of the price is the wine itself.
Not true. Duty, tax, packaging and margins are fixed or proportional, so on cheap bottles they make up most of the price.
Spending a little more often buys a lot more wine. Moving from 6 to 12 pounds can more than triple the value of the liquid in the bottle, since fixed costs stay the same.
What mainly drives the price of the most expensive wines?
At the top, prices follow reputation, scarcity and demand.
Price includes grapes, making, packaging, duty, tax and margins
Fixed costs dominate the price of cheap wine
Top prices follow scarcity and demand

Restaurants usually mark wine up two to four times the shop price. Margins are often highest on the cheapest wines and lowest on expensive ones in percentage terms. Wine by the glass carries higher margins to cover waste. Some restaurants allow you to bring your own bottle, for a corkage fee.
Two to four times the shop price

Good lists are organised by style or region, with vintages and producers. Look for lesser-known regions and grapes, which are often better value than famous names. The second cheapest wine is a classic choice, and restaurants know it, so it's not always the best value.
Lesser-known regions are often better value
Where are you most likely to find value on a wine list?
Famous names carry a premium. Less familiar regions and grapes usually offer more quality for the price.

A sommelier selects, stores and serves wine, and recommends pairings. Give them a price range and a style you like; it's their job to help. When a bottle is presented, check the label, then taste for faults, not preference. You can refuse a faulty bottle, but not one you simply don't like.
Give a budget and a style
What is the right thing to check when a sommelier pours a taste?
That it's the wine you ordered
That it's at a sensible temperature
The tasting is to check for faults, not personal preference.
Restaurants mark wine up two to four times
Lesser-known regions often give the best value
Tell the sommelier your budget and style; taste for faults
Explain what makes a fine wine collectable

Collectable wines age well and have a track record of price growth. Top Bordeaux, Burgundy, Champagne, Barolo, vintage Port and a few others dominate. The Liv-ex index tracks prices of these wines like a stock market. Only a tiny share of the world's wine, well under 1%, trades this way.
A tiny share, mainly a few regions

En primeur, or futures, is a way of buying Bordeaux and some other wines before they are bottled. Châteaux release a share of the wine in spring after the harvest, through négociants. Buyers pay in advance and receive bottles about two years later. The idea is to secure scarce wine at a lower price, but recent prices have often risen little after release.
Pay now, receive in two years
Buying Bordeaux before it is bottled is called en ____.
En primeur lets buyers secure wine early, through the Bordeaux négociant system.

A collectable bottle's value depends on provenance: where it has been stored and by whom. Professional bonded warehouses keep wine at steady temperatures and record each movement. Wine fraud exists: the 2012 case of Rudy Kurniawan, who faked old Burgundies, showed how hard verification can be.
Provenance, the record of how a bottle was stored, affects its value.
Yes. Buyers pay more for wine with a clear, professional storage history.
A few regions dominate fine wine collecting
En primeur lets buyers pay early for Bordeaux
Provenance and storage protect value, and fraud exists
Explain the effects of climate change on wine

Harvests in many regions are two to three weeks earlier than in the 1980s. Alcohol has risen and acidity fallen. Extreme events, like frost after early budburst, hail, heatwaves, drought and wildfire, are more common. Smoke taint from fires affected California and Australia in 2020.

Producers plant later-ripening grapes, higher or cooler sites, change canopy management for shade, and use drought-tolerant rootstocks. Regulations are changing too: in 2021, Bordeaux approved six new grapes, including Touriga Nacional, for trial in its AOCs. New regions like southern England, Tasmania and Denmark are rising.
Which are adaptations to a warming climate?
In heat, growers usually keep leaves to shade grapes, not remove them.

Glass bottles are the biggest part of wine's carbon footprint, often around 40%. Lighter bottles, bag-in-box, cans and paper bottles cut emissions. Shipping wine in bulk and bottling near the market also helps. Many producers now measure their footprint and seek certification.
What is usually the largest part of wine's carbon footprint?
Heavy glass bottles account for a large share of emissions, often around 40%.
Climate change brings earlier harvests and more extreme weather
Producers adapt with new grapes, sites and rules
Lighter packaging cuts wine's biggest footprint, glass
Everything from The Business of Wine
Explain how wine is sold and priced
Match each term to its meaning.
These terms describe how wine is sold and valued.
Why do cheap wines have little liquid value?
Fixed costs like duty and packaging make up most of the price
Duty, tax, packaging and margins weigh heavily on cheap bottles.
When tasting a wine in a restaurant, you may send it back if you simply dislike it.
Not true. The tasting checks for faults. Disliking a sound wine isn't grounds to refuse it.
Which are effects of climate change in vineyards?
Acidity tends to fall, not rise, with heat.
In the US, the system separating producers, wholesalers and retailers is called the three-____ system.
The three-tier system dates from the end of Prohibition in 1933.
Wine moves through producers, importers and retailers
Price reflects costs at first, then scarcity
Fine wine relies on provenance; en primeur sells it early
Climate change pushes new grapes, sites and packaging
